cues.text: Innocent III's Grand Design
By the early thirteenth century, Pope Innocent III stood at the height of medieval papal authority.

During his pontificate, he asserted the Church's role in governing Christendom's kingdoms while confronting heresy in southern France and the fractured aftermath of the Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople.
Determined to address both the reform of the Church and the recovery of the Holy Land in a single, comprehensive assembly, he issued the summoning bull Vineam Domini in April 1213.
Bishops thus had more than two years to prepare and travel.
The long lead time produced the largest and most representative council the Church had yet seen.
When it opened at the Lateran on November 11, 1215 , Innocent presided over seventy-one patriarchs and metropolitans.
These included the Latin Patriarchs of Constantinople and Jerusalem, installed after the Fourth Crusade, along with four hundred and twelve bishops and some nine hundred abbots and priors.
Envoys of nearly every major ruler in Europe also attended.
Defining Transubstantiation
The council's first and most theologically significant canon offered a formal exposition of Catholic faith.
For the first time in a conciliar document, it included the technical term transubstantiation .
This term described how the bread and wine of the Eucharist become the Body and Blood of Christ while retaining their outward appearances.
The canon also condemned the pantheistic teachings of Amaury of Bène and censured aspects of the apocalyptic theology of Joachim of Fiore .
A further canon required every Catholic of the age of discretion to confess their sins to their own priest at least once a year .

It also required them to receive Holy Communion at least during the Easter season—the origin of what later devotional practice would call the “Easter duty,” a minimum standard of sacramental life still recognizable in Catholic practice today.
Confronting Heresy and Regulating Society

Building on Third Lateran's earlier, more measured response to dissent, the council issued detailed procedures for identifying, trying, and punishing heretics and their protectors, part of the broader campaign against Catharism then underway in the form of the Albigensian Crusade.
It also addressed the practical governance of the Church, ordering the establishment of cathedral schools and mandating that provincial councils meet annually to enforce reform.
Among its more controversial provisions, the council required Jews and Muslims living in Christian territory to wear distinctive dress.
This was intended to prevent inadvertent intermarriage or social mingling with Christians.

The canon's long and painful afterlife in later centuries of discriminatory legislation stands in uncomfortable tension with the council's own stated pastoral concerns, and later eras of the Church have explicitly repudiated it.
A New Crusade
Innocent III used the council's final sessions to promote a new crusading expedition to recover the Holy Land.
He decreed a four-year truce among Christian rulers, directing resources and manpower eastward instead of toward wars among Christians themselves.
This call would eventually bear fruit, after Innocent's own death in 1216, in the Fifth Crusade.
The council also took up long-standing disputes over ecclesiastical precedence and jurisdiction across the Latin and newly established Latin-rite Eastern territories.
It attempted — with only partial success — to regularize relations between the Roman and Greek clergies after the Fourth Crusade's conquest of Constantinople.
Legacy
Fourth Lateran is widely regarded by historians as the most important council of the Church between Chalcedon in 451 and Trent in the sixteenth century.
This reflects both the sweep of its seventy canons and the scale and diversity of its attendance.
Its formal use of "transubstantiation" shaped Eucharistic theology for the rest of the medieval period and beyond.
Its requirement of annual confession and Communion had a direct and lasting effect on the ordinary religious practice of medieval and modern Catholics alike.
Often simply called "the Great Council" by medieval canonists, it represents the high-water mark of papal authority and conciliar ambition in the High Middle Ages.
It addressed doctrine, discipline, crusade policy, and the social regulation of a genuinely pan-European Christian society in a single assembly.
